title.en: Functions of Several Variables & Partial Derivatives

body.en: A function of two variables \( f(x,y) \) assigns a number to every point of a region in the plane — think of it as a surface, or a landscape with \( f \) as elevation. A partial derivative measures how that surface tilts if you walk in only one coordinate direction at a time, holding the other fixed. Everything in this track builds from that one idea.

A function \( f:D\to\mathbb{R} \) with \( D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2 \) assigns a real number \( f(x,y) \) to each point \( (x,y)\in D \). Its graph \( z=f(x,y) \) is a surface in \( \mathbb{R}^3 \). Fixing \( y=b \) and letting \( x \) vary traces a curve on that surface — the "trace" in the direction of \( x \) — and similarly for fixing \( x=a \).

The partial derivative of \( f \) with respect to \( x \) at \( (a,b) \) is \[ f_x(a,b)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a,b)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h,b)-f(a,b)}{h}, \] and similarly \( f_y(a,b)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(a,b+h)-f(a,b)}{h} \). In practice: to find \( f_x \), differentiate with respect to \( x \) treating \( y \) as a constant; for \( f_y \), treat \( x \) as a constant.

value.en: \( f_x(a,b) \) is the slope, in the \( x \)-direction, of the tangent line to the trace curve through \( (a,b,f(a,b)) \)
\( f_{xx}=\partial(f_x)/\partial x \), \( f_{xy}=\partial(f_x)/\partial y \), \( f_{yx}=\partial(f_y)/\partial x \), \( f_{yy}=\partial(f_y)/\partial y \)
The vector \( \nabla f=(f_x,f_y) \) packages both partials — the subject of Chapter 2

body.en: The two "mixed" second partials, \( f_{xy} \) and \( f_{yx} \), are computed in opposite orders — yet for every function you'll meet in this course they come out equal. That's not a coincidence; it's a theorem, and it's what makes multivariable calculus's bookkeeping (Hessians in Chapter 3, curl and divergence beyond this track) manageable.

label.en: ▲ Theorem 1.1 — Clairaut's Theorem (equality of mixed partials)

body.en: If \( f_{xy} \) and \( f_{yx} \) both exist near \( (a,b) \) and are continuous at \( (a,b) \), then \[ f_{xy}(a,b)=f_{yx}(a,b). \]

Fix \( (a,b) \), and for small nonzero \( h,k \) consider the mixed second difference \[ \Delta(h,k)=f(a+h,b+k)-f(a+h,b)-f(a,b+k)+f(a,b). \]

Route 1: \( x \) first, then \( y \). Let \( g(t)=f(t,b+k)-f(t,b) \), so \( \Delta(h,k)=g(a+h)-g(a) \). Since \( f_x \) exists, \( g \) is differentiable with \( g'(t)=f_x(t,b+k)-f_x(t,b) \); by the Mean Value Theorem, \[ \Delta(h,k)=h\,g'(a+\theta h)=h\big[f_x(a+\theta h,b+k)-f_x(a+\theta h,b)\big] \] for some \( \theta\in(0,1) \). Since \( f_{xy} \) exists, apply the Mean Value Theorem again — this time in \( y \), to the function \( s\mapsto f_x(a+\theta h,s) \) — to get \[ \Delta(h,k)=hk\,f_{xy}(a+\theta h,\,b+\psi k) \] for some \( \psi\in(0,1) \).

Route 2: \( y \) first, then \( x \). The identical argument with the roles of \( x \) and \( y \) swapped — starting from \( \Delta(h,k)=\big[f(a+h,b+k)-f(a,b+k)\big]-\big[f(a+h,b)-f(a,b)\big] \) — gives \[ \Delta(h,k)=hk\,f_{yx}(a+\theta' h,\,b+\psi' k) \] for some \( \theta',\psi'\in(0,1) \), using that \( f_y \) and \( f_{yx} \) exist.

Both routes compute the same quantity \( \Delta(h,k) \), so dividing by \( hk\neq0 \): \[ f_{xy}(a+\theta h,\,b+\psi k)=f_{yx}(a+\theta' h,\,b+\psi' k) \] for every small nonzero \( h,k \). As \( h,k\to0 \), both evaluation points approach \( (a,b) \), so continuity of \( f_{xy} \) and \( f_{yx} \) at \( (a,b) \) gives \[ f_{xy}(a,b)=\lim_{h,k\to0}f_{xy}(a+\theta h,b+\psi k)=\lim_{h,k\to0}f_{yx}(a+\theta' h,b+\psi' k)=f_{yx}(a,b). \]

Verify \( f_{xy}=f_{yx} \) for \( f(x,y)=x^3y^2+\sin(xy) \).

\( f_x=3x^2y^2+y\cos(xy) \), so \[ f_{xy}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\big[3x^2y^2+y\cos(xy)\big]=6x^2y+\cos(xy)-xy\sin(xy). \]

\( f_y=2x^3y+x\cos(xy) \), so \[ f_{yx}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big[2x^3y+x\cos(xy)\big]=6x^2y+\cos(xy)-xy\sin(xy). \]

Identical, exactly as Theorem 1.1 guarantees — both \( f_{xy} \) and \( f_{yx} \) are continuous everywhere here (polynomials and \( \sin,\cos \) of polynomials), so the theorem applies at every point.
